defaults.teacher_persona: A manager of managers who has introduced AI tools into two teams and keeps the focus on the work, the people, and the evidence.
classmates: A team lead worried about workload and blame
A finance partner who asks what the change costs and what it returns
defaults.interaction: Leadership simulation: the teacher models a decision, then the peers take opposing roles and defend a position with the evidence at hand.
defaults.assessment: Each classroom ends with 3-5 checks aligned to the chapter's graded activity.

classrooms.title: The Manager's AI Map
classrooms.prompt: Have the class map where AI already touches a team's work, whether or not it was approved: drafting, summarizing, scheduling, screening, reporting, and the shadow use on personal accounts. The teacher separates activity from value and risk, then the peers plot their own team's uses on a value-versus-risk grid and identify the one that most needs a decision. Include slides on the four portfolio questions (value, risk, capability, accountability), a roleplay where a team member admits to pasting client data into a personal account, and a quiz on which use needs a stop order first.
objectives: Map approved and shadow AI use in a team
Place uses on a value-versus-risk grid
Decide which use needs a stop order

classrooms.title: Process Improvement, Not Tool Envy
classrooms.prompt: Take a team process with a real bottleneck and work it as an improvement project: measure the current state, separate waste from necessary work, choose assist-or-redesign, and define the new measure. The teacher shows an automation that saved a step and created two new reviews, and the peers calculate whether the change is actually a net gain. Include slides on process waste, a roleplay where a vendor demo promises a 40% saving, and a quiz on which change should be piloted first. Keep every number traceable to the class's own estimate.
objectives: Measure a process before changing it
Test whether a change is a net gain after new reviews

classrooms.title: People: Roles, Skills, and Resistance
classrooms.prompt: Work the human side of an AI change: which tasks shift, which roles grow, what training is required, how performance is measured during the transition, and how to answer the fear of being replaced. The teacher models a team conversation, then the peers role-play a resistant senior employee and a junior employee who is over-relying on the tool. Include slides on task-level change and honest communication, a roleplay on redundancy rumours, and a quiz on which response builds trust. Emphasize: no productivity target without a training plan and a review gate.
objectives: Explain task-level change without false reassurance
Pair every target with training and review
Respond to resistance with evidence, not slogans

classrooms.title: The Business Case, the Vendor, and the Rules
classrooms.prompt: Build a one-page business case for the team's chosen change: cost, expected benefit, evidence quality, risk, owner, and the decision being asked for. Then run a vendor review: what data leaves, where it is processed, retention, subprocessors, accuracy claims, exit, and who is accountable for an error. The teacher shows a case that ignored review labor and a vendor answer that dodged retention. The peers red-team each other's cases. Include a roleplay where procurement wants a signature this week and a short assessment on which case is decision-ready.
objectives: Write a business case with evidence quality stated
Ask the vendor the questions that decide risk
Identify who is accountable when the tool errs

activities.title: A case a director can decide
